summary: Universal Manifest is a portable signed identity envelope: a JSON-LD document carrying who a person, agent or device is, what they consent to, and pointers to the heavier things they own, signed with a profile called Signature Profile A. That profile is Ed25519 over RFC 8785 canonical JSON with the signature member removed, and the key is named by a URI reference that must resolve. The envelope never hosts anything; pointers exist so that heavy files stay where they are. Around that core sits a published document set: a primer, a Tier-0/Tier-1 base specification, three tier extensions, an optional-features profile and a cookbook, with per-version conformance fixtures. Version 0.3 is named as the stable published reference and 0.4 as the production-candidate milestone, dated 9 July 2026, under the W3C Software and Document Licence with the Universal Manifest Working Group as editors. It is the only subject in this group with both a written specification and a real conformance suite, and the project's own implementation verifies byte for byte against the reference validators. Three things a standards audience should hold onto. First, the base is a boundary model: six stages run on arrival, a receipt is written, and nothing re-checks during a live session; the bilateral session model is published as preview. Second, the previous claim that nobody outside this stack had adopted it is no longer true, and this is the largest change in this file: the public TeleportXR repositories accept a Universal Manifest address in place of an avatar URL, verify Signature Profile A, gate each facet on the subject's consent with default-deny, and return a receipt. Third, only trust tier zero, signature-only, is verified by that implementation, and verification is explicitly not proof that the presenter is the subject.

coverage.note: The signature block names its verification key by URI reference and the specification requires that reference to be present, recommending a decentralized identifier URL or an HTTPS URL. An embedded public key may travel beside it for offline verification, but the reference itself must still resolve. A third-party implementation states the reason plainly: accepting an inline key without checking it against the reference is exactly what would let an attacker re-sign a modified document with their own key.

coverage.note: This is the subject's core and it is now published in full. Signature Profile A is the baseline normative profile: RFC 8785 canonical JSON with the signature member removed, signed with Ed25519, the value base64url without padding. The evaluator checklist is ordered and mandatory, and a manifest whose only signature uses an unsupported profile is rejected rather than accepted quietly. The context document is pinned by its own content hash, so the meaning of the terms cannot be swapped underneath a verifier.

coverage.note: The base model is still an evaluation of a presented document rather than an interactive request-and-present protocol, and the interactive parts, holder binding and presentation proof, live in a companion profile with several sections still marked preview. But the older reading of this row, that the three specifications it would present to all leave the slot empty and no plug is specified, is no longer true. One of the three now has a plug: the public TeleportXR repository accepts a manifest address in place of an avatar URL, resolves it, verifies Signature Profile A, and answers with a receipt. A live replay weakness found in the project's own reciprocal-control holder binding, and fixed locally by binding the full content hash, was never delivered upstream; that remains a project-local record.

coverage.note: Permission is expressed as consent records inside the signed envelope, each naming the operations it allows, the purpose it allows them for, and a validity window; a separate pointer type declares delegated session authority for an agent. The evaluation rule is default-deny and it is normative: a facet with no consent entry governing it is recorded as consent-missing, and an evaluator must not process facet data when required consent is absent, expired or withdrawn. Every decision, allow or refuse, is recorded in a structured receipt.

coverage.note: Selective disclosure is a normative stage of the evaluation sequence rather than an add-on: the evaluator must extract only the facets, claims, pointers and device entries relevant to its processing context, and the specification calls this the bounded selective minimum disclosure profile. Beneath it sit encrypted facets, sealed with JSON Web Encryption inside the envelope, where a facet the evaluator cannot open must be acknowledged as present but unread rather than guessed at or treated as a failure. The stronger tracks, zero-knowledge proofs and unlinkable disclosure, are published as preview and should not be counted as shipping.

coverage.note: Universal Manifest signs with Ed25519 over RFC 8785 canonical JSON, bound to a key named by a decentralized identifier. The RP1 fabric it points at signs with a compact JSON Web Signature, RS256 and an X.509 chain. A verifier for one cannot verify the other, and the project's integration resolved that by refusing to merge them: the bridge is a pointer from the manifest to the fabric URL, never a re-signing. They answer different questions, who the person is and who published these bytes, and both are needed. The public specification states the profile; the framing of it as deliberately not a JSON Web Signature, and the bridge decision, are the project's own record.

coverage.note: The binding is real but it is generic, and a working group should know which half is standardised. The specification defines a typed pointer array: every pointer must carry a type and a target, the pointers sit inside the bytes the signature covers, and an evaluator meeting a pointer type it does not recognise must record it and must not act on it. It names no avatar pointer. The avatar meaning comes from a published fixture set and from a third-party implementation, both of which use the pointer name portableIdentity.avatar. So a destination can check that this person really claims this avatar, and it learns nothing about what the avatar file contains.

coverage.note: One thing is addressed by hash and it is the right one: the JSON-LD context document is named by a content hash, that hash is normative for context integrity, and the optional-features profile fixes the hash function as SHA-256 in multihash form. So the meaning of every term in the envelope is pinned to exact bytes. The envelope's own pointers out to heavy files remain plain locations; the base pointer requires a target URI and does not require a digest.

coverage.note: A manifest is fetched from an address, or resolved from a short identifier by a hosted resolver, and the manifest points onward at the things it describes. The resolver is a locator and nothing more: a third-party implementation records that although the resolver serves a one-minute HTTP cache header, consumers must enforce the manifest's own lifetime regardless of HTTP caching, so resolution and trust stay separate steps.

coverage.note: Agents are a first-class subject of the envelope rather than an afterthought. A manifest's subject may be a person, an agent, a device or an organisation; a pointer type declares delegated session authority, so an agent can carry evidence that it acts for someone; and the scope vocabulary in the optional-features profile includes participating in a spatial session on the subject's behalf. What is not here is any agent behaviour, lifecycle or runtime; the envelope says who is acting and under what authority, and stops there.

coverage.note: Versioning is explicit and the honesty about its cost is unusual. Each version has its own document set, its own context URL and its own conformance fixtures, v0.3 is named as the stable published reference and v0.4 as the production-candidate milestone, and the specification states outright that while the line is still 0.x a minor bump may include breaking changes in a new version folder.
